Matteo Valsecchi wins Il Lombardia alone in the rain
He attacked on the last climb, 18 kilometres from Bergamo, and nobody followed.
A rider climbing alone on a wet mountain road in the rain

It had rained since the start in Como, and by the last climb there were eleven riders left in front. Matteo Valsecchi looked at none of them. He stood on the pedals at the steepest hairpin, rode away, and crossed the line in Bergamo forty two seconds clear with his arms still on the bars.

It is his first Monument, at 31, in the race he watched from the roadside as a boy. "I did not raise my arms because I did not believe it," he said. "I thought someone would come back."

## Six hours of water

The race never had a calm hour. The descents off the Ghisallo and the Sormano were slick enough that the favourites rode them with their hands on the brakes, and a crash on the way down to the lake took out four riders who had started the day as contenders.

Valsecchi's team kept him at the back of the front group for most of the afternoon. "We wanted him out of the wind and out of trouble," said his directeur sportif, Erik Lindqvist. "That was the whole plan. The rest was him."

> I had looked at that hairpin every day for a month. I knew if I went there, nobody would want to follow in the wet.

## The hairpin

The attack came eighteen kilometres from the finish, on the second to last bend of the final climb. Nobody reacted for almost ten seconds. By the time the chase organised itself, Valsecchi was out of sight in the mist.

Behind him, Jonas Aalberg and Pablo Ibarra traded turns all the way down the descent and into Bergamo's old town. They never saw him again until the podium.

## What happens next

Valsecchi's season ends here. He said he will spend the winter at home in Lecco, ride the same roads without a number on his back, and come back in March for Milano Sanremo.

Spain come back from two down to win the Nations League final
Two goals in the last eleven minutes, then penalties in Lisbon. Lucía Ortega scored the last kick.
Spain players in red running towards their goalkeeper after the winning penalty

With eleven minutes left in Lisbon, Spain were two goals down and the stadium had started to sing the home songs. Forty minutes later, Lucía Ortega walked to the spot for the fifth penalty, waited for the whistle and put the ball in the top corner.

It was the kind of final that nobody in the Spanish camp will describe the same way twice. Elena Garmendia, the coach, called it "the worst eighty minutes and the best half hour" of her time in charge.

## Eighty minutes of nothing

For most of the night Spain looked tired. The passing that carried them through the group was slow, the full backs stayed deep and the hosts scored twice from the same move down the left, once before half time and once just after.

Garmendia made three changes on the hour. None of them worked straight away. "I was not thinking about the trophy any more," she said afterwards. "I was thinking about how to lose with some dignity."

> We stopped playing the way we planned and started playing the way we play in the park. That is when it turned.

## Eleven minutes

The first goal came from a corner that should never have been given. Marina Prats met it at the near post and the ball went in off the goalkeeper's shoulder. Four minutes later Ainhoa Etxeberria ran from the halfway line, past two players, and finished low with her weaker foot.

Extra time was nervous and almost silent. Both sides had chances, neither took them, and by the end most of the players were walking.

## The shoot-out

Spain went first and scored their first four. The hosts missed their third. Ortega, who had only come on in the 110th minute, asked to take the last one.

"She told me in the huddle," Garmendia said. "I did not argue. When a player asks for that one, you let her."

## What happens next

The squad flies home on Thursday. The league restarts at the weekend, and nine of the starting eleven play for clubs with games on Saturday. Qualification for the next World Cup begins in February.
